item.title: WhatsApp introduces new parental controls for teens
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: WhatsApp is rolling out optional parental controls covering teen privacy settings, group alerts, Channels, Status and Meta AI while keeping messages end-to-end encrypted.
item.content:encoded:
WhatsApp is introducing optional parental controls for teen accounts, giving families tools to manage privacy, group activity, Channels, Status and the Meta AI experience without giving parents access to the content of personal messages or calls.

The controls are designed to be set up by parents and teens together. WhatsApp said the tools are intended to give families more control over how teens use the service while keeping personal communications protected by end-to-end encryption.

Privacy settings and group alerts

Parents will be able to choose privacy settings such as who can see a teen’s profile photo or add the teen to groups. If the teen later wants to relax one of those settings, WhatsApp will require approval through a parent-set PIN.

Parents can also choose to receive notifications when a teen joins or leaves a group, or when a group the teen belongs to grows meaningfully in size.

Channels, Status and Meta AI

The controls extend to how teens use Channels and Status. Parents can choose how their teen can use Channels, which Status updates they can see, and who can see the teen’s own Status updates.

For Meta AI, parents can choose between WhatsApp’s default 13+ setting and a stricter Limited Content option.

WhatsApp said all of the controls are optional and can be adjusted or switched off. Even when they are enabled, personal messages and calls remain end-to-end encrypted, meaning parents and WhatsApp cannot read or listen to the content of those conversations through the parental-control feature.

Broader family controls

The teen controls follow WhatsApp’s Parent Managed Accounts feature for pre-teens. The company said it plans to continue developing the parental-control tools based on feedback from families.

Philippines, Meta agree on child-safety measures and rapid-response group after Zamboanga shooting

item.title: US’ First Solar sues China’s JA Solar, Vietnam unit over solar cell patent
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: The US-based solar cell maker First Solar has sued Chinese rival JA Solar and the US-based distributor American Panel Solutions, alleging they infringed its patent on making TOPCon solar cells
item.content:encoded:
The US-based solar cell maker First Solar has sued Chinese rival JA Solar and the US-based distributor American Panel Solutions, alleging they infringed its patent on making TOPCon solar cells.

In a statement on Thursday, First Solar said the case is the latest step in its campaign to enforce the patent against Chinese manufacturers.

First Solar said it filed the suit on October 1 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware. It accused JA Solar and American Panel Solutions of infringing U.S. Patent 9,130,074. The patent covers methods of making tunnel Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact (TOPCon) crystalline silicon photovoltaic solar cells.

Notably, First Solar made accusations against JA Solar and its Vietnamese unit JA Solar Vietnam Co., Ltd, while JA Solar is operating manufacturing bases in China, Vietnam, and Malaysia.

The case extends a push First Solar began in 2024, after it said it owned a TOPCon patent portfolio acquired through its 2013 purchase of TetraSun and opened infringement investigations into several crystalline-silicon makers.

It has since sued China’s JinkoSolar and others and filed a complaint with the U.S. International Trade Commission naming about 10 companies, including JA Solar.

The patent First Solar is asserting faces challenges. In May, China’s patent office invalidated the ‘074 patent, striking down all its claims in a case brought by JinkoSolar. The patent is also under reexamination in the United States, with JinkoSolar and Canadian Solar seeking to have it declared invalid.

The dispute reflects tension between First Solar, the largest U.S.-based solar manufacturer, which uses thin-film technology, and Chinese companies that dominate production of crystalline-silicon panels.

In its most recent quarter, First Solar’s net income rose 23 percent from a year earlier to $423 million, even as net sales slipped 4 percent to about $1.06 billion. The company passed 100 GW of cumulative module sales and held a contracted order backlog of about 45 GW running through 2030.

First Solar reaffirmed its 2026 forecast of $4.9 billion to $5.2 billion in net sales and 17-18 GW of modules sold. Its profits lean heavily on U.S. manufacturing tax credits, projected at more than $2.1 billion this year.

China’s JinkoSolar terminates $1.5B project in Vietnam due to US tariff on PV panels

item.title: Singapore students divert 892 kg of waste in 6-week sustainability program
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: More than 120 Singapore tertiary students diverted 892 kilograms of food and plastic waste over six weeks in national sustainability program SG Eco Loop 2.0.
item.content:encoded:
More than 120 Singapore tertiary students diverted 892 kilograms of food and plastic waste over six weeks in national sustainability program SG Eco Loop 2.0.

In a statement on Friday, the program organizer said the event aims to lift low recycling rates. SG Eco Loop 2.0, run by the nonprofit Singapore Deep-Tech Alliance, concluded with a public showcase on October 2.

It drew 37 student teams from 12 institutes of higher learning, each given a S$200 ($155) budget and an industry mentor to build and test a waste-reduction prototype. It is funded by a government eco-fund under the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment and catalysed by the Temasek Foundation OSCAR Fund.

The “biggest impact” prize went to team SCOBYS for turning kombucha-brewing waste into a biomaterial and using black soldier fly larvae to convert food waste into fertilizer and animal feed, diverting 420 kilograms.

A “best innovation” prize went to Foodprint, for an automated return kiosk for campus vending machines. Both teams received S$1,000 and up to six months of support to deploy their ideas.

Singapore generated about 1.7 million tonnes of food and plastic waste in 2025 and recycled only about a tenth of it, the organizer said. The program added food waste this year, alongside plastic, and expanded from a 2025 pilot of 100 students at a single college.

Over two years, the program reached 4,000 students and diverted 10,000 kilograms of waste, with backing from companies including Lenovo.

Clara Chen, a director of the Singapore Deep-Tech Alliance, said meeting Singapore’s recycling targets needed grassroots solutions rather than market-led innovation alone.

Singapore launches standard on sustainability excellence to strengthen business competitiveness

item.title: Southeast Asia divided over AI’s environmental impact – ISEAS survey
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: Public opinion across Southeast Asia is divided over artificial intelligence (AI)’s environmental impact, with 47.9 percent of respondents viewing AI positively but 30.2 percent holding negative views, while 21.9 percent say they lack enough knowledge to assess its environmental costs and benefits, a survey launched by the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute showed on Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Public opinion across Southeast Asia is divided over artificial intelligence (AI)’s environmental impact, with 47.9 percent of respondents viewing AI positively but 30.2 percent holding negative views, while 21.9 percent say they lack enough knowledge to assess its environmental costs and benefits, a survey launched by the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute showed on Thursday.

According to the Southeast Asia Climate Outlook Survey Report 2026, regional respondents are more likely to view AI positively, with 27.2 percent seeing it as somewhat good and 20.7 percent as clearly good, than negatively, with 17.2 percent seeing it as somewhat bad and 13 percent as clearly bad.

However, 21.9 percent say they do not know enough about AI’s environmental costs or benefits to judge, indicating that public understanding of its footprint is still developing.

Respondents in Laos (45.7 percent), Cambodia (33.7 percent), and Vietnam (33.1 percent) are most likely to view AI as clearly good for the environment.

Those from Brunei are the most sceptical: 35.4 percent see AI as clearly bad, while only 1 percent view it as clearly good.

Uncertainty is also uneven. Around a third of respondents in Myanmar (35.6 percent) and Brunei (31.8 percent) lack sufficient knowledge to judge, compared with approximately a fifth in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.

Education shows a clear pattern respondents’ choices. Respondents with the highest education levels are least likely to regard AI as clearly good: 11.4 percent of master’s degree holders and 11.8 percent of doctoral degree holders, compared with 38 percent of those with no formal education and 36.1 percent with primary education.

Bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degree holders are also more sceptical, with between a third and nearly half seeing AI as somewhat or clearly bad for the environment.

This suggests that greater familiarity with AI, and possibly its energy demands, is associated with more critical assessments of its environmental impact.

Meanwhile, rising energy prices and the cost of living dominate the region’s concerns regarding its transition to renewable energy and the phase-down of fossil fuels (44.6 percent).

This is followed by concerns over energy shortages as the second major issue (26.1 percent).

Cambodia stands out as the main exception, where concerns over energy shortages (36.9 percent) slightly exceed concerns over rising energy prices and the cost of living (35.9 percent).

Brunei is another notable outlier. The country records the highest proportion of respondents who do not foresee negative impacts from the energy transition (26.1 percent), more than three times the ASEAN average (7.6 percent).

Compared with the 2024 survey, the share of respondents concerned about rising energy prices and the cost of living fell from 52.4 percent in 2024 to 44.6 percent in 2026.

At the same time, concern over energy shortages increased steadily, from 20.3 percent in 2024 to 26.1 percent in 2026.

In general, these concerns might reflect the energy shock disruptions caused by geopolitical events in the preceding years.

Concern over rising energy prices and the cost of living generally increases with age. The share of respondents mentioning this issue increases from 38.6 percent among respondents in the youngest age group (16–21) to 49.7 percent in the oldest age group (above 60).

By contrast, younger respondents are more concerned about job losses and widening social inequality, decreasing from 14.4 percent for both issues among those aged 16–21 to 7.1 percent and 6.5 percent, respectively, among the oldest age group

Majority of regional respondents (65 percent) view solar energy as an energy source with the greatest clean potential.

Hydropower ranks second at 33 percent, followed by bioenergy at 27.4 percent and wind energy at 25.8 percent.

Compared with 2024, solar continues to retain first and hydropower second place. Bioenergy, previously labelled “biofuels”, has risen from seventh place, at 14.1 percent, to third (27.4 percent), while wind energy fell from third to fourth place (25.8 percent).

Solar is the leading choice in nine countries: Brunei (48.7 percent), Cambodia (56.7 percent), Indonesia (61.3 percent), Malaysia (75.7 percent), the Philippines (77.1 percent), Singapore (74.9 percent), Thailand (76.9 percent), Vietnam (71.2 percent), and Timor-Leste (66 percent).

Hydropower is Laos’s (55.6 percent) and Myanmar’s (63.8 percent) top choice.

The increase in support for bioenergy should be interpreted cautiously. The broader term used in the 2026 survey explicitly encompasses renewable energy derived from organic materials, including crops, wood, and organic waste.

As a result, direct comparison with the narrower 2024 “biofuels” category is imperfect. This increase may also reflect heightened energy-security concerns, including energy supply disruptions linked to the Strait of Hormuz crisis, renewing regional interest in securing domestic, near term fuel alternatives.

At the country level, higher support for bioenergy in Malaysia (34.7 percent), Indonesia (34.3 percent), Thailand (33.2 percent), and Cambodia (31.4 percent) may reflect interest in agricultural residues, biomass, and waste-to-energy plants.

Wind energy continues to be viewed more positively by countries that possess this resource including Vietnam (47.1 percent) and Timor-Leste (37.3 percent). It is incidentally TimorLeste’s second choice.

Green hydrogen has fallen from fourth place in 2024 (16.5 percent) to fifth place in 2026 (13.8 percent).

Geothermal energy remains at sixth place increasing modestly from 11 percent in 2024 to 12.4 percent.

Interest in nuclear energy gained marginally from 10.8 percent to 11.8 percent with Singapore registering a higher than regional average interest at 31.4 percent, an increase of 11.1 percent from 2024.

Tidal energy continues to place last albeit with an increase from 8.1 percent in 2024 to 10.7 percent this year.

The survey also showed that carbon taxation is recognized as a potential policy instrument to support decarbonization.

Across the region, 62 percent of respondents support the introduction of a national carbon tax, compared with 19.6 percent who oppose it.

Support is particularly strong in Vietnam (83 percent), Indonesia (72.8 percent), and Thailand (68.3 percent).

Singapore remains the region’s most trusted potential climate leader, with confidence dipping slightly to 39.9 percent in 2026 (from 42.9 percent in 2024) even as Singapore respondents’ own confidence in their country rose to 77.3 percent, likely buoyed by its Year of Climate Adaptation designation and S$5 million ($3.91 million) adaptation package committed by its government.

Indonesia holds a distant second at 11.1 percent, while Vietnam has overtaken Thailand for third place at 9.1 percent, driven by rising domestic confidence (up to 49.5 percent) in their own government’s follow-through on their 2050 net-zero pledge.

Overall, unemployment and economic recession (55.3 percent) and climate change/extreme weather (53.6 percent) rank as Southeast Asia’s top two public concerns, separated by just 1.7 points, with domestic
political instability (46 percent) close behind.

Climate concerns top the list in the Philippines, Vietnam, Singapore and Malaysia—consistent with the Philippines’ and Vietnam’s high exposure to disaster risk—while economic concerns dominate in Indonesia, Brunei, Timor-Leste, Thailand and Cambodia.

Regional respondents identify insufficient financial resources (15.8 percent) as the biggest obstacle to decarbonization, followed closely by the lack of research and development (R&D), technology and expertise (14.8 percent) and insufficient alternative energy resources (14.4 percent).

Notably, energy insecurity caused by geopolitical events (e.g. war in Ukraine, US-China rivalry) has surged to 13.4 percent — more than double its 2024 level (5.3 percent) — despite remaining below the top-tier capacity constraints.

This sharp increase signals growing awareness across the region that external geopolitical dynamics are increasingly entangled with domestic energy transition pathways, particularly in Singapore (20.3 percent) and Indonesia (17.3 percent).

At the country level, Brunei (25.8 percent) and Singapore (25.1 percent) stand out for citing insufficient alternative energy resources as the most significant impediment, reflecting the structural constraints faced by smaller, fossil-fuel-dependent or land scarce economies.

Cambodia (22.1 percent) and Vietnam (22 percent) continue to flag R&D and technological limitations as their primary bottleneck.

The 2026 survey gathered the views of 3,706 respondents from eleven ASEAN member states. It is the first time that this survey has included respondents from Timor-Leste, ASEAN’s newest member.

Singapore AI adoption could lift potential output 1.06 percent in long run – AMRO

item.title: Vietnam to host SEMIEXPO chip exhibition in December, drawing global firms
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: Vietnam will host SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026, an international semiconductor exhibition, in Ho Chi Minh City on December 13-14, drawing some 200 companies and global chip leaders,
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam will host SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026, an international semiconductor exhibition, in Ho Chi Minh City on December 13-14, drawing some 200 companies and global chip leaders,

The event organizers, namely Vietnam’s National Innovation Center and SEMI Southeast Asia, a global semiconductor-industry association, announced the event on Thursday. The event will serve Vietnam’s target of moving up the global semiconductor supply chain.

Now in its third year, SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026 is expected to feature about 170 booths and around 200 international firms, the organisers said.

The global association’s president, Ajit Manocha, is due to attend, along with executives from chip and equipment makers including NVIDIA, Cadence, Synopsys, Coherent, and Tokyo Electron.

Organisers said this year’s edition shifts from mainly showcasing technology, as in the previous two, toward connecting Vietnamese companies directly with the needs of large manufacturers. The aim is to help local firms become second- and then first-tier suppliers in global chip supply chains, said Vo Xuan Hoai, deputy director of the National Innovation Center.

Vietnam is pursuing a semiconductor strategy with 2030 targets of at least 100 chip-design companies, one small fabrication plant and 10 packaging-and-testing facilities, plus more than 50,000 engineers and graduates, and a domestic market exceeding $25 billion. The country already hosts about 100 semiconductor firms across design, packaging and testing, with Samsung, SK, Amkor, and Intel expanding there.

The exhibition comes as the global semiconductor market is forecast to reach about $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion in 2026 and to exceed $2 trillion before 2030, according to industry data cited by the organizers.

Vietnam will host SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026, an international semiconductor exhibition, in Ho Chi Minh City on December 13-14, drawing some 200 companies and global chip leaders,

item.title: BTSE Bhutan announces final license for virtual asset trading, custody in Gelephu
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: BTSE Bhutan has announced its final Financial Services License for virtual asset trading and custody in Gelephu Mindfulness City.
item.content:encoded:
BTSE Bhutan has announced that it has received a Financial Services License from the Gelephu Financial Services Office, moving the virtual-asset trading company beyond the in-principle approval TNGlobal covered in May.

The license covers operation of a multilateral trading facility for virtual assets and custody services within the Gelephu Mindfulness City Special Administrative Region in southern Bhutan.

The GFSO’s public financial-institutions directory lists BTSE Exchange Pte. Ltd. as active for both activities. The directory gives an effective date of July 24, 2026, while BTSE publicly announced the final license on September 29.

Trading and custody authorized

BTSE Bhutan said the final license confirms that it has satisfied the conditions attached to its earlier in-principle approval.

Under the GFSO framework, the company is authorized to operate a multilateral trading facility and provide custody for virtual assets. BTSE said client assets will be held under its licensed custody arrangements.

Yew Chong Quak, CEO of BTSE Bhutan, said the company will now focus on launching trading services while expanding its offering in phases and maintaining compliance and security requirements.

BTC and ETH spot trading planned first

BTSE Bhutan plans to begin onboarding users in the coming weeks. Its initial spot markets are expected to be BTC/USDT and ETH/USDT, with additional crypto trading pairs to follow subject to the company’s listing framework and regulatory requirements.

The company also plans to introduce fiat on-ramp and off-ramp services later in the rollout, including support for moving between US dollars and virtual assets.

Building a local presence in Gelephu

BTSE Bhutan said it has appointed key personnel since receiving in-principle approval and is building out its presence in Gelephu. The company plans to establish a local office and hire local talent as operations expand.

Gelephu Mindfulness City is a special administrative region that Bhutan is developing as an economic hub with its own regulatory framework. The GFSO maintains a public directory of approved financial institutions operating under that framework.

Virtual asset trading firm BTSE Bhutan approved for financial services license in Gelephu Mindfulness City

item.title: PRECISE, Temus form center to support Singapore’s genome program’s Phase III
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: Singapore's national precision-medicine agency (PRECISE) and Temasek-backed technology firm Temus will jointly build the data and computing systems for the next phase of the country's effort to sequence hundreds of thousands of residents' genomes.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s national precision-medicine agency (PRECISE) and Temasek-backed technology firm Temus will jointly build the data and computing systems for the next phase of the country’s effort to sequence hundreds of thousands of residents’ genomes.

In a statement on Friday, PRECISE said the two have signed a memorandum of understanding to establish a five-year PRECISE-Temus Joint Innovation Centre supporting Phase III of Singapore’s National Precision Medicine program. The signing, at a precision-health event, was witnessed by Health Minister Ong Ye Kung.

Phase III, launched in November 2025 and running to 2031, aims to sequence the whole genomes of about 450,000 residents, or a tenth of Singapore’s resident. It can build on 100,000 sequenced in the previous phase and test the use of genomic data in clinical care at scale.

The center will develop shared platforms to process and analyze whole-genome data and build safeguards for handling it securely, the partners said. It builds on work the two have done since 2024 on a genomics data system that handles about 13.6 PB of data. It is upgrading past 60 PB, cutting processing times from weeks to days.

The center also aims to train specialists in fields such as computational biology and bioinformatics. For Temus, the project is a healthcare use of its “AI Foundry,” part of a national AI program under which it is hiring and deploying Singapore-based AI professionals.

Japan’s Mitsui taps Singapore’s Oncoshot for AI oncology-data platform across IHH hospital network

item.title: SoundHound powers Kia Sorento generative AI in India
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: SoundHound AI has deployed its conversational voice and generative AI technology in Kia's Sorento for India, supporting cabin control and live queries.
item.content:encoded:
SoundHound AI has deployed its voice and generative artificial intelligence technology in the Kia Sorento sold in India, giving the sport utility vehicle a conversational assistant that can control cabin systems, answer vehicle questions and retrieve live information.

The California-based voice AI company announced the deployment on September 30. Kia’s India website separately lists a real-time generative AI assistant among the Sorento’s connectivity features and identifies SoundHound as the service provider for online voice recognition.

Assistant handles vehicle controls and live searches

The system responds to the wake phrase “Hey Kia” and supports multi-turn conversations, according to SoundHound. Drivers can use natural-language requests to adjust climate controls, cabin lighting, windows and driving modes without relying on fixed command phrases.

Passengers can also ask the assistant questions about the vehicle using information from the digital owner’s manual. SoundHound said the assistant can explain features such as hybrid powertrain functions and seating settings, while its search functions provide point-of-interest navigation, news and contextual question-and-answer responses.

Kia India’s Sorento product page describes the assistant as capable of understanding questions, maintaining a conversation and returning real-time answers. The same page lists voice command support alongside over-the-air software updates for vehicle controllers, connected services and driver-assistance features.

SoundHound described the India deployment as the global debut of the Kia AI Assistant with real-time generative AI in the Sorento lineup. The supplier did not disclose the commercial terms of its agreement with Kia, expected vehicle volumes or a revenue contribution from the rollout.

Voice data is processed by SoundHound

Kia’s privacy disclosures provide additional detail about how the service operates. Its India privacy policy says online voice recognition transfers voice samples to SoundHound and its subprocessors, which may be located outside India, so the requests can be converted into text, interpreted and returned to the vehicle.

For the Kia AI Assistant, Kia says voice commands are transmitted to SoundHound in real time to process requests and generate responses. The automaker classifies the relevant information as pseudonymized identifiers, usage-based data and recording data, and says the feature can be disabled through the vehicle’s head-unit settings.

That disclosure is significant because generative AI in vehicles combines convenience features with continuous network services and data processing. The effectiveness of the assistant will depend not only on language understanding but also on response latency, cabin-noise handling, connectivity and the accuracy of information returned to drivers.

Automakers expand conversational AI in Asia

The Sorento deployment extends SoundHound’s automotive business into another large Asian vehicle market. The company positions its OASYS platform as a system for building and operating conversational agents across cloud and embedded environments, including vehicles and smart devices.

Six days before the Sorento disclosure, SoundHound introduced OASYS Edge, an architecture intended to run language-model-powered voice agents on vehicle and device hardware. The company says local processing can keep some functions available without continuous network access and reduce the data sent to cloud services. SoundHound expects deployments of that embedded product to begin later in 2026.

Kia is also developing its broader software-defined vehicle strategy through Hyundai Motor Group. The group has outlined plans for next-generation infotainment systems with large-language-model-based voice assistants and over-the-air updates across Hyundai, Kia and Genesis vehicles.

For SoundHound, the India launch supplies a visible production reference for its automotive technology. For Kia, it adds a branded generative AI feature to a flagship sport utility vehicle rather than limiting the technology to a demonstration or future model plan.

Hyundai Motor Group Redefines In-Vehicle Experience with ‘Pleos Connect’ Next-Generation Infotainment System

item.title: Seeing Machines demonstrates real-time 3D human understanding for Physical AI on NVIDIA Jetson Thor
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Seeing Machines says its Human Mesh Recovery technology can reconstruct people in 3D in real time on NVIDIA Jetson Thor, targeting robotics and Physical AI systems that operate around humans.
item.content:encoded:
Australia-based Seeing Machines has published a technical paper showing that its Human Mesh Recovery technology can reconstruct a detailed 3D representation of a person in real time on NVIDIA Jetson Thor hardware, extending its human-sensing work into robotics and other Physical AI systems.

The company said the system uses a single camera view to estimate a person’s location, posture and movement, allowing machines to interpret human motion locally rather than relying on a remote cloud connection. Seeing Machines is positioning the capability for environments such as factories, hospitals, warehouses and other settings where robots and people operate in close proximity.

3D human understanding moves to embedded hardware

High-fidelity 3D human reconstruction has typically required substantial computing resources, which can make real-time use on embedded systems difficult. Seeing Machines said its Human Mesh Recovery, or HMR, model is designed to balance accuracy, inference speed and model efficiency so that the workload can run at the edge.

According to the technical paper, HMR was demonstrated on NVIDIA Jetson Thor, with the company arguing that the result shows detailed 3D human reconstruction can be performed in real time on embedded hardware. The model supports both standard RGB cameras and RGB-D cameras without increasing its parameter count.

Local processing matters for robotics because delays in understanding a person’s position or movement can affect how quickly a machine responds. For systems operating around people, that can influence both usability and safety.

Seeing Machines extends automotive human sensing into robotics

The HMR work is part of the broader Physical AI Platform that Seeing Machines launched in August. The platform builds on the company’s experience in driver and occupant monitoring and applies similar human-centered perception concepts to robotics and industrial automation.

Paul McGlone, CEO of Seeing Machines, said robots working around people need to understand more than whether a person is simply present. The company is focusing on the combination of location, posture and movement so that machines can respond to changing human behavior in real time.

The company said HMR is one capability within a wider platform that combines computer vision, human-behavior modeling and safety-oriented AI. Seeing Machines has spent more than two decades developing human-sensing systems for automotive, commercial fleet, aviation, rail and off-road applications.

Physical AI competition shifts toward human-machine interaction

As Physical AI systems move from controlled demonstrations into workplaces and other environments shared with people, perception requirements become more demanding. Object detection can tell a robot that a person is nearby, but not necessarily how that person is moving, whether they are reaching into a work area or how their posture is changing.

Seeing Machines is betting that richer 3D human understanding can become part of the perception stack for robots that need to operate safely and naturally around people. Its latest paper focuses on whether that level of scene understanding can be delivered within the compute and latency constraints of embedded hardware rather than depending on cloud processing.

The company has published the technical paper, titled “Real-time 3D Human Mesh Recovery at up to 180 FPS on NVIDIA Jetson Thor,” alongside a demonstration video.

Seeing Machines launches Physical AI Platform to power the next generation of humanoid robots

item.title: IMDA partners TikTok to develop local microdrama expertise and fuel a new pipeline of original IP
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: Singapore’s media professionals will be given support to develop microdrama expertise across live-action and artificial intelligence (AI)-animated formats, under a new IMDA-TikTok Microdrama Program jointly launched by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and TikTok Singapore.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s media professionals will be given support to develop microdrama expertise across live-action and artificial intelligence (AI)-animated formats, under a new IMDA-TikTok Microdrama Program jointly launched by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and TikTok Singapore.

The program brings together IMDA’s commitment to strengthening local media talent with TikTok’s deep audience and market insights – helping media professionals build new production capabilities, create original intellectual property (IP), and develop strategies to commercialize their stories, IMDA said in a statement on Thursday.

As part of IMDA’s Digital Content and Capability Development (DCCD) program launched earlier this year, this new initiative will equip media professionals with the skills and tools to develop and produce 50 to 100 episodes, each one to three minutes long, taking their creative ideas from concept to market.

The first run will benefit media professionals from 20 accredited companies, with the potential to scale to a wider pool in future editions.

Microdramas and other short-form vertical video content are a fast-growing format, with the global market projected to generate $150 billion in revenue this year.

Today, 87 percent of people in Singapore aged 15 and above access top social media video sites such as TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook on a weekly basis, with an increasing share of that time spent watching and engaging with short-form content.

As audience behaviors continue to evolve, strong characters, compelling storytelling and emotional resonance remain at the heart of commercially successful stories.

Against this backdrop, the program gives participants hands-on experience in developing and producing microdramas rooted in Singapore’s culture and perspectives, through mentorships, workshops and masterclasses.

Over a span of six to nine months, participants will learn microdrama storytelling techniques from TikTok and their partners, such as vertical content production, shot design and composition, storytelling cliffhanger design and responsible use of technology, including AI.

Meanwhile, two training tracks will be available for their choosing.

Firstly, live-action track focuses on content filmed with live actors, locations and sets, designed for mobile viewing and with the option to supplement content using Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) or AI-assistance.

Secondly, AI-enabled animation track focuses on animated content such as anime or comic-style animation using AI tools. Training here will extend to prompt engineering, character consistency planning, visual effects (VFX) quality review, and the use of Seedance 2.5 – an advanced AI video generation platform by TikTok’s parent company ByteDance.

Capability development remains central to the IMDA-TikTok Microdrama Program, said the statement.

The program is designed to strengthen participants’ existing storytelling abilities while introducing new commercial and platform-specific capabilities, including prompt engineering, paywall strategies, and audience monetization, drawing on TikTok’s market insights and expertise.

Beyond the final output, participants will be onboarded onto TikTok’s wider content ecosystem, gaining access to the full content journey – from delivery and distribution to audience engagement – alongside bespoke consultancy to help their Made-with-Singapore stories reach global markets.

“IMDA is excited to partner with TikTok to equip our media professionals with the skills to create compelling Singapore-made microdrama for global audiences,

“With TikTok’s reach and insights, our talent and companies are well-placed to seize new opportunities on a global platform, harnessing new tech tools with the same care and craft they bring to any creative work. This partnership is an important step towards building a vibrant, globally competitive media sector,” said Yvonne Tang, Assistant Chief Executive at IMDA’s Media Industry Group.

Candera Chan, Public Policy Lead for Singapore and ASEAN, said TikTok is proud to partner with IMDA to grow Singapore’s microdrama ecosystem and equip our local media industry with the capabilities to capture new opportunities in this fast-growing format.

“By combining Singapore’s creative talent with TikTok’s global reach and expertise in short-form storytelling, we can help made-in-Singapore content reach audiences around the world. We look forward to deepening our partnership with IMDA and the industry to build a vibrant and globally connected creative ecosystem,” she added.

Ultimately, the IMDA-TikTok Microdrama Program combines IMDA’s commitment to building the capabilities of Singapore’s media ecosystem with TikTok’s influence as a global launchpad for media and entertainment talent.

This will help create opportunities for Singapore’s media professionals to better connect with audiences across formats, both locally and internationally, said the statement.

Singapore launches world’s first liquid cooling standard for data centers in tropical climates
